See McMurry v. Stanley, 69 Tex. 227, 6 S. W. 412; Stewart v. Stewart, .61 N.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A term used in the Spanlsh law, denoting the act by which the bound-arles of an estate or portion of a country are determined.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. Persons deprived of memory, white, New Recop. b. 1, tit. 2, c. 1, g 4.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): or DESPATCH. A mes-ttage, letter, or order sent with speed on affairs of state; a telegraphic message.

What is due process? Due process (or due process of law) primarily refers to the concept found in the Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution, which says no one shall be "deprived of life, liberty or property without due process of law" by the federal government. The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, uses the same eleven words, called the Due Process Clause, to extend this obligation the the states. These words have as their central promise an assurance that all levels of American government must operate within the law ("legality") and provide fair procedures.

Due process protects persons affected by governmental adjudication through requirements of appropriate authority, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The required protection depends on the setting and the interests at risk.

The duty of care is a concept that arises in both agency law and tort law, and refers generally to an obligation (or duty) imposed on an individual (or individuals) to behave in a certain way, often qualified by a standard of “reasonableness”. In agency law, the duty of care is a fiduciary duty requiring directors and officers of a corporation to make decisions that pursue the corporation’s interests with reasonable diligence and prudence. This fiduciary duty is owed by directors and officers to the corporation, not the corporation’s stakeholders or broader society.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A horse equipped with saddle and furniture.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A maple tree. Not to be confounded with ara bills, (arable land.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tbe followers of Erastus. The sect obtained much influence in England, particularly among common lawyers in the time of Selden. They held that offenses against religion and morality should be pun-lshed by the civil power, and not by the cen-sures of the church or by excommunication, wharton.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The obliteration of words or marks from a written instrument by rubbing, scraping, or scratching them out. Also the place in a document where a word or words.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. To be divided. Judicium familia erciscunda, a suit for the partition of an inheritance. Inst. 4, 17, 4.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Raising up; building; a completed building. In a statute on the "erection” of wooden buildings, this term does not Include repairing, alteration, enlarging, or removal. See Shaw v. Hitchcock, 119 Mass. 256; Martine v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Therefore; hence; because.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civU law. Undertakers of work; contractors. Cod. 4, 50.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A term of the Irish Brehon law, denoting a pecuniary mulct or recompense which a murderer was judicially condemned to pay to the family or relatives of his victim, it corresponded to the Saxon “weregild.” See 4 Bl. Comm. 313.

The rule of Erie Railroad v. Tompkins that a federal court hearing state-law claims applies state substantive law and federal procedural law, and that there is no federal general common law. Later cases (Guaranty Trust, Byrd, Hanna) supply tests for classifying a rule as substantive or procedural.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): we erect one of tbe words by which a corporation mny be created in England by the king’s charter. 1 Bl. Comm. 473.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): By metonymy, this term is used to describe the ofiice or functions of a judge, whose state robe, lined with ermine, is emblematical of purity and honor without stain, webster.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. The loose scattered ears of corn that are left on the ground after the binding.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The gradual eating away of the soil by the operation of currents or tides. Distinguished from submergence, which is the disappearance of the soil under the water and the formation of a navigable body over it. Mulry v. Norton, 100 N.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old lnw. A waif or stray; a wandering beast Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat Error. Used in the Latin formula for assigning errors, and in the reply thereto, “ln nullo est erratum,” i. e., there was no error, no error was committed.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Involving error; deviat-ing from the law. This term is never used by courts or law-writers as designating a corrupt or evil act Thompson v. Doty, 72 Ind. 338.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Erroneously; through error or mistake.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A mistaken judgment or incorrect belief as to the existence or effect of matters of fact, or a false or mistaken conception or application of the law.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: An error not resisted is approved.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: An error made by a clerk ought not to injure; a clerical error may be corrected.

terms.term: Errores ad sua principia referre, est refellere
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: To refer errors to their origin is to refute them.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A meeting of the neighborhood to compromise differences among themselves; a court held on the boundary of two lands.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): AR. In the Roman law. A cognomen in the Gens Julia, whlch was nssumed by the successors of Julius. Tayl.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old law. A cutting off the branches or boughs of trees. Cowell; Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To scald. It is said that to scald hogs was one of the ancient tenures in serjeanty. wharton.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A writ of exchange. A license in the shape of » a writ, formerly granted to an English merchant to draw a bill of exchange on another.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An old English law term, signifying exchange.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The departure or deliverance out of custody of a person who was lawfully Imprisoned, before he is entitled to his liberty by the process of law.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Engllsh law. Delivered from that punishment which by the laws of the forest lay upon those whose beasts were found upon forbidden laud. Jacob.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): That which comes by chance or accident Cowell.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In fendal law. Escheat is an obstruction of the course of descent, and consequent determination of the tenure, by some unforeseen contingency, in which case the land naturally results back, by a kind of reversion, to the original grantor, or lord of the fee. 2 Bl. Comm. 15; wallace v. Harin-stad, 44 Pa. 501; Marshall v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In English law. The name of an officer who wus appointed in every county to look after the escheats which fell due to the king in that particular county.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A jnry or inquisition.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A tax formerly paid in boroughs and corporations towards the support of the community, which is called “scot and lot.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. An offl-cer, resembling a notary in French law, who has authority, to set down in writing, und verify by hls attestation, transactions and contracts between private persons, and also judlclal acts and proceedings.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. A written instrument Every deed that is made by the hand of a public escribano, or notary of a corporation or council (concejo,) or sealed wlth the seal of the king or other authorized persons, white, New Recop. b. 3, tit. 7, c. 5.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Fr. Fraud, swlnd-ling, cheating.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. An es-crow; a scroll. “And deliver the deed to a stranger, as an escrowl.” Perk. c. 1, $ 9; Id. c. 2, H 137, 138.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Service of tlie shield, one of tbe varieties of tenure in knight's service.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An old term for the products which the ground or land yields; as the hay of the meadows, the herbage of the pasture, corn of arable fields, rent and services, etc. The word has been anciently applied to the land itself. Jacob; Fosgate v. Hydraulic Co., 9 Barb.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A scroll; a writing; a deed. Particularly a deed delivered by the grantor into the hands of a third person, to be held by the latter until the happenlng of a con-tlngency or performance of a condition, and then by him delivered to the grantee. Thorn-as v. Sowards, 25 wis. 631; Patrick v.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): RO. Suits in the ecclesiastical courts for spiritual offenses against conscience, for non-payment of debts, or breaches of civil contracts. This attempt to turn the ecclesiastical courts into courts of equity, was checked by the consti-tntions of Clarendon, A. D. 1164. 3 Bl.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): RP. A thing surrendered into the hands or power of another; a thing given or delivered. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Robbers, or destroyers of other men’s lands and. fortunes. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Sbippage, or passage by sea. Spelled, also, "skippeson" Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tackle or furniture ; outfit Certain towns in England were bound to furnish certain ships at their own expense and with double skippage or tackle. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old law. A hireling of servile condition.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Seniority; the condition or right of the eldest; the prlvilege of the eldest-born. Particularly used of the privilege of the eldest among coparceners to make a first choice of purparts upon a voluntary partition.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): ln Spanish law. A junction of all the serrate papers made In the course of any one proceeding and which remains in the office at the close of it. Castillero v. U.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A period of tlme fixed by law or by a court within which certaln acts are to be performed, e. g., the production of papers, payment of debts, etc.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A mutual promise between a man and a woman to marry each other at some other time. It differs from a marriage, because then the contract is completed. wood, Inst. 57.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In English law. A tide of dignity next above gentleman, and below knight. Also a title of office given to sheriffs, serjeants, and barristers at law, justices of the peace, and others. 1 Bi. Comm. 406; 3 Steph.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. To cut down woods to clear land of trees and underwood; properly to thin woods, by cutting trees, etc., at intervals. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): woodlands turned into tillage by uprooting the trees and removing the underwood.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): That whlch is indispensable to that of whlch It is the essence.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A writ to he quit of toll; it lies for citizens and burgesses of any city or town who, by charter or prescription, ought to be exempted from toll, where the same is exacted of them. Reg. orig. 258.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): It is to be understood or known; “it is to-wit.” Lltt. g$ 9, 45, 46, 57, 59. A very common expression In Littleton, especially at the commencement of a section; and, according to Lord Coke, “lt ever teacheth us some rule of law, or general or sure leading point" Co. Lltt. 16.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Violence may also put on the mask of law.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: It is the part of a good judge to extend the jurisdiction.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): This word occurs frequently in the constitution of the United States, and it is there used in different meanings: (1) To settle firmly, to fix unalterably ; as to establish justice, which is the avowed object of the constitution. (2) To make or form; as to establish a uniform ruie of naturalization, and uniform laws on the subject of bankruptcies, which evidently does not mean that these laws shall be unalterably established as Justice.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An ordinance or statute. Especlally used of those ordinances or statutes passed in the reign of Edw. I. 2 Inst. 156; Britt. C. 21.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A bridge or stank of stone or timber. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. In Spanish America this was a measure of land of sixteen square varas, or yards. 2 white, Recop. 139.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. Delay in a voyage, or in the delivery of cargo, caused by the charterer or consignee, for which demurrage is payable.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. A standard, (of weights and measures.) So called because it stands constant and immovable, and hath all other measures coming towards it for their conformity. Termes de la Ley.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): ER L’ESTATE. A species of release which inures by way of enlarging an estate, and conslsts of a conveyance of the ulterior Interest to the particular tenant; as lf there he tenant for life or years, remainder to another in fee, and he in remainder releases all his right to the particular tenant and hls heirs, this gives him the estate in fee. 1 Steph. Comm. 518.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of estate less than freehold, where lands and tenements are let by one man to another, to have and to hold at the will of the lessor; and the tenant by force of thls lease obtains possession. 2 Bl. Comm. 145; 4 Kent, Comm. 110; Lltt $ 68. or it is where lands are let without limiting any certain and determinate estate. 2 Crabb, Real Prop. p. 403, $ 1543.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate whereby the creditor, under the custom of London, retained the possession of all his debtor’s lands until his debts were paid. 1 Greenl. Cruise, Dig. 515.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tenant by the curtesy of Eugland is where a man survives a wife who was seised in fee-simple or fee-tail of lands or tenements, and has had issue male or female by her bom alive and capable of inheriting the wife’s estate as heir to her; in which case he will, on the decease of his wife, hold the estate during hie life as tenant by the curtesy of England. 2 Crabb, Real Prop. $ 1074.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A freehold ee-tate, not of inheritance, but which is held by.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of estate less than freehold, where a man has an lnterest in lands and tenements, and a possesslon thereof, by virtue of such interest, for some fixed and determinate period of time; as in the case where lands are let for the term of a certain number of years, agreed upon between the lessor and the lessee, and the lessee enters thereon. 1 Steph. Comm. 263, 264. Blackstone calls this estate a “contract” for the possession of lands or tenements for some determinate period. 2 Bl. Comm. 140.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate in lands held by two or more persons, wlth interests accruing nnder dlfferent titles; or accruing under the same title, hut at different periods; or conferred by words of limitation Importing that the grantees are to take in distinct shares. 1 Steph. Comm. 323.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate which several persons hold as one heir, whether male or female. This estate has the three unities of time, title, and possession; but the interests of the coparceners may be unequal. 1 washb. Real Prop. 414; 2 Bl. Comm. 188.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of life-estate which a woman is, by law, entitled to clalm on the death of her husband, in the lands and tenements of whlch he was seised in fee during the marriage, and which, her issue, lf any, might hy possibility have inherited. 1 Steph. Comm. 249 ; 2 Bl. Comm. 129; Cruise, Dig. tit 6; 2 Crabb, Real Prop, p. 124, 1117; 4 Kent, Comm. 35.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The estate which a man has where 'lands are given to him and to his heirs absolutely without any end or limit put to his estate. 2 Bl. Coram. 106; Plowd. 557; 1 Prest. Est. 425; Lltt. i 1. The word “fee,” used alone, is a sufll.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate in lands or tenements granted to two or more persons, to hold in fee-simple, fee-tall, for life, for years, or at will. 2 Bl. Comm. 180; 2 Crabb, Real Prop. 937. An estate acquired by two or more persons in the same land, by the same title, (not being a title by descent,) and at the same period; and without any limitation by words importing that they are to take in distinct shares.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate whereby a present Interest passes to and resides in the tenant, not depending on any subsequent circumstance or contingency. 2 Bl. Comm. 163. An estate where the tenant is in actual pernancy, or receipt of the rents and other advantages arising therefrom.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate limited to take effect in possession, or in enjoyment, or in both, subject only to any term of years or contingent interest that may intervene, immediately after the regular expiration of a particular estate of freehold previously created together with it, by the same instrument, out of the same subject of property. 2 Fearne, Rem. § 159; 2 BL Comm. 163; 1 Greenl. Cruise, Dig. 701.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of estate in expectancy, created by opera^ tlon of law, being the residue of an estate left in the grantor, to commence in possession after the determination of some particular estate granted out by him. 2 Rl. Comm. 175; 2 Crabb, Real Prop. p. 978, 8 2345. The residue of an estate left in the grantor or his heirs, or in the heirs of a testator, commenc-lng in possession on the determination of a particular estate granted or devised. 1 Rev. St N.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate held by a person in his own right only, with out any other person being joined or connected with him in point of interest, during his estate. This is the most common and usual way of holding an estate. 2 Bl. Comm. 179; Cruise, Dig. tit. 18, c. 1, $ 1.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate in gage or pledge. 2 Bl. Comm. 157; 1 Steph. Comm. 282.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An estate in land or other real property, of uncertain duration; that is, either of inheritance or which may possibly last for the life of the tenant at the least, (as distlngulshed from a leasehold;) and held by a free tenure, (as distinguished from copyhold or villelnage.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of freehold estate in lands, otherwlse called a “fee,” where the tenant is not only entitled to enjoy the land for his own llfe, hut where, after his death, it is cast by the law upon the persons who successlvely represent him in perpetuum, in right of blood, ac cording to a certaln establlsbed order of descent. 1 Steph. Comm. 218; Lltt $ 1; Nellis v. Munson, 108 N. Y. 453, 15 N.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Estate for another’s life. An estate in lands which a man holds for the life of another person. 2 Bl. Comm. 120; Lltt 56.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The lords spiritual, the lords temporal, aud the commons of Gveat Britain. 1 Bl. Comm. 153. Sometimes called the “three estates.”

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): This word is used to express the mind or judgment of the speaker or writer on the particular subject under consideration. It implies a calculation or computation, as to estimate the gain or loss of au enterprise. People v. Clark, 87 Hun (N.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To stop, bar, or Impede; to pre vent; to preclude. Co. Litt 352a.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A bar or impedlment raised by the law, which precludes a man from alleging or from denying a certain fact or state of facts, in consequence of his previous allegation or denial or conduct or admission, or in'consequence of a final adjudication of the matter in a court of law. Demarest v. Hopper, 22 N. J.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A wrlt for a wlfe judicially separated to recover her all-mony or estovers, obsolete.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An allowance made to a person out of an estate or other thlng for hls or her support, as for food nnd raiment.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Cattle whose owner is ur-known. 2 Kent, Comm. 359; Spelman; 29 Iowa, 437. Any beast, not wild, found with-In any lordship, and not owned by any man. Cowell; 1 Bl. Comm. 297.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Straightened, as applied to roads. Cowell.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To strip; to despoil; to lay waste; to commit waste upon an estate, as by cutting down trees, removing buildings, etc. To injure the value of a reversionary interest by stripping or spoiling the estate.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of aggravated waste, by stripping or devastating the land, to the injury of the reversioner, and especlally pending a suit for possession.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And it is adjourned. A phrase used in the old reports, where the argument of a cause was adjourned to another day, or where a second argument was had. 1 Keb. 692, 754, 773.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An abbrevlation for et alii, “and others.”
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And others on the other side. A phrase constantly used in the Tear Books, in describing a joinder in issue. P. 1 Edw. II.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And another. The abbrh-viation et al. (sometimes in the plural written et als.) is affixed to the name of the persou first mentioned, where there are several plaintiffs, grantors, persons addressed, etc.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And others; and other things; and so on. In its abbreviated form (etc.) this phrase is frequently affixed to one of a series of artlcles or names to show that others are intended to follow or understood to be included. So, after reciting the initla-tory words of a set formula, or a clause already given in full, etc. is added, as au abbreviation, for the sake of convenience. See Lathers v.

terms.term: et de ceo se mettent en le pays
terms.definition: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. And of this they put themselves upon the country.

terms.term: et de hoc ponit se super patriam
terms.definition: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And of this he puts himself upon the country. The formal conclusion of a common-law plea in bar by way of traverse. The literal translation is retained in the modern form.

terms.term: et habeas ibi tunc hoc breve
terms.definition: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And have you then there this writ The formal words directing the return of a writ. The literal translation is retained in the modern form of a considerable number of writs.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And this he is prepared to verify. Tbe Latin form of concluding a plea in confession and avoidance.

terms.term: et hoo petit quod inquiratur per patriam
terms.definition: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And this he prays may be inquired of by the country. The conclusion of a plaintiff's pleading, tendering an Issue to the country. 1 Salk. 6. Literally translated in the modem forms.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And he had it A common phrase in the Year Books, expressive of the allowance of an appllcatlon or demand by a party. Pam. demanda la view. Et habuit, etc. M. 6 Edw.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat - And not A technical phrase in pleading, which introduces the negative averments of a special traverse. It has the same force and effect as the words "absque hoc," and is occasionally used instead of the latter.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An abbrevlation for et sequen-tto, “and the following.” Thus a reference to “p- 1. et seq." means “page first and the following pages.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And so. In the Latin forms of pleading these were the introductory words of a special conclusion to a plea in bar, the object being to render it positive and not ar-gumentative; as et sic nil debet.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): And so it hangs. A term used in the old reports to signify that a point was left undetermined. T. Raym. 168.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An abbreviation for et uxor,— “and wife.” where a grantor’s wife joins.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The code of honor agreed on by mutual un-1 derstanding and tacitly accepted by members of the legal profession, especially by the bar.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. ways, walks, or hedges. Blount.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in going and returning. Applied to vessels. 3 C. Rob. Adm. 141.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat Going, remaining, and returning. A person who is privileged from arrest (as a witness, legislator, etc.) is generally so privileged eundo, morando, et redeundo; that is, on his way to the place where his duties are to be performed, while he remains there, and on his return journey.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Equal laws and a well-ad-justed constitution of government.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A male of the human species who has been castrated. See Domat, llv. prel. tlt. 2, $ 1, n. 10. Eckert v. Van Pelt, 69 Kan. 357, 76 Pac. 909, 66 L.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In old practlce. An escape from prison or custody. Reg. orig. 312.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A subtle endeavoring to set aside truth or to escape the punishment of the law. This wlll not be allowed. If one person says to another that he will not strike him, but wlll glve him a pot of ale to strike first, and, accordingly, the latter strikes, the returning the blow is punishable; and, if the person first striking is killed, it is murder, for no man shall evade the justice of the law by such a pretense. 1 Hawk. P.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tendlng or seeking to evade; eluslve; shifting; as an evasive argument or plea.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. The dellvery at even or night of a certain portion of grass, or com, etc., to a customary tenant, who performs the service of cutting, mowing, or reaplng for hls lord, given him.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In reference to judicial and quasi judicial proceedings, the “event" means the conclusion, end, or finai outcome or re-suit of a litigation; as, in the phrase “abide the event,” speaking of costs or of an agreement that one suit shall be governed by the determination in another. Reeves v. Mc Gregor, 9 Adol. A El. 576; Benjamin v.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Each one of all; the term includes all the separate individuals who constitute the whole, regarded one by one. Geary v. Parker, 65 Ark. 521, 47 S. W. 238; Purdy v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In tbo civil law. To recover anything from a person by virtue of the judgment of a court or judicial sentence.
Information presented in testimony or in documents that is used to persuade the fact finder (judge or jury) to decide the case in favor of one side or the other.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A term applied to written Instruments or securities for the payment of money, importing on their face the existence of a debt 1 Rev. St N. Y. p. 599, 8 55.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A deed or other document establishing the title to property, especially real estate.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French law. The withdrawal of a cause from the cognizance of an inferior court, and bringing it before another court or judge. In some respects this process resembles the proceedings upon.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Dispossession by process of law; the act of depriving a person of the possession of lands which he has held, in pursuance of the Judgment of a court. Rea-soner v. Edmundson, 5 Ind. 395; Cowdrey v. Colt, 44 N.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Havlng the quality of evldence; constituting evidence; evidencing. A term introduced by Bentham, and, from Its convenience, adopted by other writers.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): (L. Fr. Etoe, water.) In old English law. Toll paid for water passage, The same as aquage.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): CE. Adultery; spouse breach; marriage breach. Cowell; Tomlins.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An office in the royal household where the table linen, etc., is taken care of. wharton.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): out of abundance; abundantly; superfluously; more than suffl-cient Calvin.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. out of abundant cautlon. “The practice has arisen abundanti cautcla.” 8 East, 326; Lord Ellenborongh, 4 Maule & S. 544.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): on the other slde. 2 Show. 461. Applled to counsel.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A phrase derlved from the clvil law, meaning, in Justlce and falrness; accordlng to w’hat is Just and good; according to equity and conscience. 3 Bl. Comm. 163.

terms.term: Ex antecedentibus et consequentibus fit optima interpretatio
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The best interpration is made from antecedents and consequents.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): By or with the consent of the court.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): By or with the consent of the father. A species of dower ad ostium ecclesia, during the life of the father of the husband; the son, by the father’s consent expressly given, endowing his wife with parcel of his father’s lands. Abolished by 3 & 4 wm. IV. c. 105, { 13.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): with his assent Formal words in judgments for damages by default Comb. 220.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): of the goods or property. A term of the civil law; dlstlngulshed from fn bonis, as being descriptive of or applicable to property not in actual possession. Calvin.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): From the chair, originally applled to the declslons of the.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): of certain or sure knowledge. These words were anciently used In patents, and imported full knowledge of the subject-matter on the part of the king.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): By color; under color of; under pretense, show, or protection of. Thus, ex colore officii, under color of office.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): From or out of. loan. A term applied in the old law of England to a right of action arising out of a loan, (oommodatum.) Glanv. llb. 10, c. 13; 1 Reeve, Eng. Law, 166.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): By a comparison of writings or handwritings. A term in the law of evidence. Best, Pres. 218.

Federalism distributes judicial and lawmaking responsibilities between the national government and the states. Procedure can affect that distribution through jurisdiction, governing law, and the treatment of state-created rights.

Boyle recognizes a defined defense to certain state design-defect claims when imposing liability would significantly conflict with federal procurement decisions. It is a specialized federal common-law doctrine.

A narrow category of state-law claims can arise under federal law when resolving the claim necessarily requires deciding an actually disputed and substantial federal issue in a manner consistent with the federal-state division of judicial responsibility.

The doctrine that federal law supersedes conflicting state law pursuant to the Supremacy Clause; may be express, implied by field occupation, or implied by conflict. Federal spending conditions may also preempt inconsistent state practices.

An attorney employed by the federal courts on a full-time basis to provide legal defense to defendants who are unable to afford counsel. The judiciary administers the federal defender program pursuant to the Criminal Justice Act.

As provided for in the Criminal Justice Act, an organization established within a federal judicial circuit to represent criminal defendants who cannot afford an adequate defense. Each organization is supervised by a federal public defender appointed by the court of appeals for the circuit.

Federal jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1331 over civil actions arising under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States. The federal issue must appear in the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint.

The daily publication of the federal government in which agencies publish proposed rules, final rules, notices, and presidential documents. Publication in the Federal Register is a step in notice-and-comment rulemaking.

terms.term: Federal rights enforced in state court
terms.definition: The reverse-Erie problem concerns the obligations of a state court adjudicating a federal claim. State procedure cannot be used in a way that impermissibly defeats the federal right and its protected incidents.
Impleader brings a nonparty into an action because that person may owe the defending party all or part of the liability asserted by the plaintiff. Common examples involve indemnity or contribution.

Rule 19 asks whether an absent person should be joined and, if joinder is not feasible, whether the action can fairly proceed without that person. The inquiry protects existing parties, absentees, and the interest in complete resolution.

Interpleader allows a stakeholder facing competing demands for the same property or obligation to bring the claimants into one proceeding. It protects against inconsistent obligations while providing a process to decide entitlement.

A class action allows named parties to litigate on behalf of an adequately defined group of absent persons when the requirements for representative litigation are satisfied. It can make small claims viable and resolve common issues together.

Intervention is a procedure by which a person outside the lawsuit seeks to enter it to protect an interest or participate under the rule’s conditions. Rule 24 distinguishes intervention of right from permissive intervention.

Summary judgment decides a claim or defense without trial when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. It examines an evidentiary record rather than only a complaint.

Statutory interpleader is a specific federal jurisdictional route for competing claims to money or property. The readings distinguish its minimal-diversity, fund, service, venue, and injunction provisions from ordinary Rule 22 interpleader.

terms.term: Federal Tort Claims Act postal-matter exception

Federal-question jurisdiction concerns actions arising under federal law within the applicable jurisdictional grant. Federal creation of the cause of action supplies the principal route, while a narrow category of state-law claims can also qualify.

A fee simple is the greatest possible property interest in land, granting its owner all traditional property rights. Because a fee simple interest stretches out in time forever, there can only be one fee simple at a time for any given chunk of land. Traditionally, transferring a fee simple required a deed with the words “to X and their heirs.” In the modern day, there is a presumption that a fee simple is transferred unless the text of a grant specifically indicates a lesser interest is transferred instead.

Overview The First Amendment of the United States Constitution protects the right to freedom of religion and freedom of expression from government interference. It was adopted into the Bill of Rights in 1791. The Supreme Court interprets the extent of the protection afforded to these rights.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A staff, used in making livery of seisin. Bract, fol. 40.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. A debt which is created, bnt which will not he-come due till a future day. 1 Bell, Comm.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): This term has grown out of those purely speculative transactions, in which there is a nominal contract of sale for.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Those who are to be. Part of the commencement of old deeds. "Sciant prcesentes et futuri, quod ego talis, dedi et concessi,” etc., (Let all men now living and to come know that I, A.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): one of the fines incurred for homicide.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A bow-net for catching fish. Pub. St Mass. 1882, p. 1291.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Scotch law. To defile; to declare foul or defiled. Hence, to find a prisoner guilty.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Scotch practlce. Fyled; found guilty.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): £ ax. In Anglo-Saxon law. The military array or land force of the whole country. Contribution to the fyrd was one of the imposts forming tbe trinoda necessitas.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old European law. A pledge. Spelman; Calvin. A custom.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An excise; a tax on movables; a rent, custom, or service. Co. Litt. 213. —Land gabel.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The Law Latin form of “gabel,” (q. v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Persons who paid gabel, rent, or tribute. Domesday; Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A rent; a tax. Domesday; Du Cange. The gable-end of a house. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Rent paid in money. Seld. Tlt. Hon. 321.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The payment of custom or tribute. Scott.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Property subject to the gaffoldgild, or liable to be taxed. Scott.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The same word as "gabel” or “gavel.” Rent; tax; interest of money.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Profits; winnings; Increment of value, Gray v. Darlington, 15 wall. 65, 21.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The gain or profit of tilled or planted land, raised by cultivating it; and the draught, plow, and furniture for carrying on the work of tillage by the baser klnd of sokemen or villeins. Bract. 1. 1. c. 9.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tillage, or the profit arising from lt, or from the beasts employed therein.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A soke-man ; one who occupied or cultivated arable land, old Nat. Brev. fol. 12.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The payment of a rent, tax, duty, or annuity.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old records. A piratical vessel; a galley.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Scotch law. Amends or compensation for slaughter. Bell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A kind of coin which, with susklns and doltkins, was forbidden by St. 3 Hen. V. c. 1.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A llquid measure, containing 231 cublc Inches, or four qunrts. The imperial gallon contalns about 277, and the ale gallon 282, cublc inches. Hollender v. Magone (C.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A scaffold; a beam laid over either one or two posts, from which malefactors are hanged.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old European law. A stroke or blow. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A child born in lawful wed-lock ; also one born to betrothed but unmarried parents. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To game or play at a game for money. Buckley v. o’NIel, 113 Mass. 193. 38 Am. Rep. 460. The word “gamble” is perhaps the most apt and substantial to convey.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Birds and beasts of a wild nature, obtained by fowling and hunting. Bacon, Abr. See Coolidge v. Choate, 11 Metc.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The act or practice of play ing games for stakes or wagers; gambling; the playing at any game of hazard. An agreement between two 6r more persons to play together at a game of chance for a stake or wager which is to become the property of the winner, and to which all contribute. In re Stewart (D. C.) 21 Fed. 398; People v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. Gains or profits resulting from the employment of property held by husband and wife in common. white, New Recop. b. 1, tlt 7, c. 5.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The time when the bounds of the parish are lustrated or gone over by the parish officers,—rogation week. Enc. Lond.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Officers in ancient times whose business it was to examine weights and measures. Skene.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A prison for temporary confinement; a jail; a place for the confinement of offenders against the law.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In criminal law. The delivery or clearing of a gaol of the prls-oners confined therein, by trying them.
A default term the UCC supplies when the parties' agreement is silent, such as a reasonable price under § 2-305 or a reasonable time for delivery under § 2-309.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): or GARANTIA. A warranty. Spelman.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French law. This word corresponds to warranty or covenants for title in English law. In the case of a sale this garantie extends to two thlngs: (1) Peaceful possesslon of the thing sold; and (2) absence of undiscloscd defects, (difauts caches.) Brown.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Lombardic law. A gift; a free or absolute gift; a gift of the whole of a thing. Spelman.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. In old English law. A warrantor of land; a vouchee; one bound by a warranty to defend the title and seisin of his alienee, or, on default thereof, and on eviction of the tenant, to give him other lands of equal value.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A bundle or sheaf. Blada in gorbis, corn or grain in sheaves. Reg. orig. 96; Bract, fol. 209.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. Tlthes of corn, (grain.) Bell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Engllsh statutes. To sort or cull out the good from the bad in spices, drugs, etc. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Servants who follow a camp. wals. 242.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): or GARDE. L. Fr. wardship; care; custody; also the ward of a city.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A small piece of land, appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers, or vegetables. People v. Greeuburgh. 57 N. Y. 550; Ferry v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Engllsh law. A guardian, defender, or protector. In feudal law, gardio. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A garden. Reg. orig. lb, 2.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. A warren; a prlvi-leged place for keeping animals.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Victuals, arms, and other Implements of war, necessary for the defense of a town or castle. Mat. Par. 1250.

One garnished; a person against whom process of garnishment is issued; one who has money or property in his possession belonging to a judgment debtor, or who owes the judgment debtor a debt, which money, property, or debt is attached in his hands, with notice to him not to delivery or pay over to the judgment debtor the amount claimed in the garnishment summons until the judgment in the suit is entered.

A statutory post-judgment proceeding in which a third party who holds property, money or credits belonging to the judgment debtor is required to surrender such property, money or credits (to the extent of the judgment) to the court or sheriff for application against the judgment awarded against the judgment debtor.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Garniture; whatever is necessary for the fortification of a city or camp, or for the ornament of a thing. 8 Rymer, 328; Du Cange; Cowell; Blount.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A method of inflicting the death penalty on convicted criminals practised in Spain, Portugal, aud some Spauish-American countries, consistiug in strangula-tion by means of an iron collar which is mechanically tightened about the neck of the sufferer, sometimes with the variation that a sharpened screw is made to advance from the back of the apparatus and pierce the base of the brain. Also, popularly, any form of strangling resorted to to overcome resist-ance or induce unconsciousness, especially as a concomitant to highway robbery.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. An amerciament or fine. Cowell.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A string or ribbon by which tlie stocking is held upon the leg. The mark of the highest order of English knighthood, ranking next after the nobility. This military order of knighthood is said to have been first instituted by Richard I., at the siege of Acre, where he caused twenty-six kDights who firmly stood by him to wear thongs of blue leather about their legs. It is also said to have been perfected by Edward III. and to have received some alterations, which were.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Scotch law. ward-er. 1 Pltc. Crim. Tr. pt 1, p. 8.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A temporary governor of the country. Blount. A bailiff or steward. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. wastel; wastel bread; the finest sort of wheat bread. Britt c. 30 i rfelham.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. waste or nncultivat-ed ground. Brltt. c. 57.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A term used in the English universities to denote double commons.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The measure of width of a railway, fixed, with some exceptions, at 4 feet 8% Inches in Great Britain and America, and 5 feet 3 inches in Ireland.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A surveying officer under the customs, excise, and internal revenue laws, appointed to examine all tuns, pipes, bogs-heads, barrels and tierces of wine, oil, and other liquids, aud to give them a mark of allowance, as containing lawful measure. There are also private gaugers In large seaport towns, who are licensed by government to perform the same duties. Rapal. & L.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A gauge or gauging; a measure of the contents of any vessel.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): ln English law. Custom; tribute ; toll; yearly rent; paymeut of revenue; of which there were anciently several sorts; as gavel-corn, gavel-malt, oat-garcl, garel-fodder, etc. Termes de la Ley; Cowell; Co. Litt. 142a.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An ancient and special kind of cessavit, used in Kent and London for the recovery of rent, obsolete. The statute of gavelet is 10 Edw. II. 2 Reeve, Eng. I4tw, c. 12, p. 298.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A species of socage tenure common in Kent, In England, where the lands desceud to all the sons, or heirs of the nearest degree, together; may be disposed of by will; do not escheat for felony; may be aliened by the heir at the age of fifteen; and dower and curtesy is given of half the land. Stim. Law Gloss.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An officer of the English crown having the general management of the mines, pits, and quarries in the Forest of Dean and Hundred of St. Brlavel’s, subject, in some respects, to the control of the com-mlssioners of woods and forests. Ile grants gales to free miners in their proper order, accepts surrenders of gales, and keeps the registers required by the acts. There is a deputy-gaveller, who appears to exercise most of the gaveller’s functions.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The official publication of the English government, also called the “London Gazette.” It is evidence of acts of state, and of everythlng done by the king in hls political capacity, orders of adjudica-tlon in bankruptcy are required to be pttb-llshed therein; and the production of a copy of the “Gazette,” containing a copy of tlie order of adjudication, is evidence of the fact Mozley & whitley.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. The ancient convention of the people to decide a cause.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An Anglo-Saxon term, meaning “conveyed.”
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. To convey; to transfer boc land, (book-land or land held by charter.) The grantor was said to gebo-cjan the alienee. See 1 Reeve. Eng.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Neighborhood or adjoining district. CowelL.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A country neighbor; an inhabitant of the same geb-urscript, or village. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. Money or tribute. A mulct, compensation, value, price. Angeld was the single valne of a thing; twigeld, doable value, etc.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Liable to pay geld; liable to be taxed. Kelham.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Taxable ; geldable.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A horse that has been castrated, and which is thus distinguished from the horse in hls natural and unaltered con.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civll law. A gem; a precious stone. Gems were distinguished by their transparency; such as ein-eralds, chrysolites, amethysts.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. A meeting or moot; a convention; a public assemblage. These were of several sorts, such, as the witena-gemot, or meeting of the wise men; the folc-gemot, or general assembly of the people; the shire-gemot, or county court; the burg-gemot, or borough court; the hundred-gemot, or hundred court; the hali-gemot, or court-baron; the hal-mote, a convention of citizens in thelr public hall; the holy-mote, or holy court; the swein-gcmotc, or forest court; the ward-mote, or ward court, wharton; Cunningham.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. A villein, or agricultural tenant, (villanus villicus;) a hind or farmer, (flrmarius rusticus.) Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil law. A son-in-law; a da ugh ter’8 husband. (Filiae vir.) Dig. 38, 10, 4, 6.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Pertaining to, or designating, the genus or class, as distinguished from that which characterizes the species or individual. Universal, not particularized; as opposed to special. Principal or central; as opposed to local, open or available to all, as opposed to select, obtaining commonly, or recognized universally; as opposed to particular. Universal or unbounded; as opposed to limited.

Personal jurisdiction over a defendant for any claim, regardless of where it arose, based on the defendant being essentially at home in the forum: domicile for an individual, and the place of incorporation and principal place of business for a corporation (Daimler AG v. Bauman).

terms.term: General jurisdiction and being at home
terms.definition: General jurisdiction permits a court to hear claims against a defendant without requiring those claims to arise from forum activity. For a corporation, the assigned cases focus on whether it is essentially at home in the forum.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The usual commons in a religious house, distinguished from pietan-tin, which on extraordinary occasions were allowed beyond the commons. Cowell.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: A general expression is to be construed generally. 8 co. 116.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: A general expression implies nothing certain.

terms.term: Generale tantum valet in generalibus, quanium singulare singulis
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: What is general prevails or is worth as much among things general, as what is particular among things particular.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: General things are to be put before particular things.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: General words are understood in a general sense.

terms.term: Generalis clausula non porrigitur ad ea quae antea specialiter sunt comprehensa
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: A general clause does not extend to those things which are previously provided for specially.
A broadly shared injury can support standing when it is sufficiently concrete and tied to the claimant; a general demand for lawful government ordinarily cannot.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Chiefs of the several orders of monks, friars, and other religious societies.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The issue or offspring of a mother-monastery. Cowell.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): May mean either a degree of removal in computing descents, or a single succession of living beings in natural descent McMillan v. School Committee, 107 N. C. 609, 12 S. E. 330, 10 L.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat Gentleman; a gentleman. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A degree of consanguinity. Spelman.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In Roman law. A tribe or clan; a group of families, connected by common descent and bearing the same name, being all free-born and of free ancestors, and in possession of full civic rights.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat People. Contra omnes gentes, against all people. Bract, fol. 37b. words used In the clause of warranty in old deeds.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Roman law. The members of a gens or common tribe.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In English law. A person of superior birth.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A woman of birth above the common, or equal to that of a gentleman; an addition of a woman's state or degree.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): As applied to notes, bonds, and other .written Instruments, this term means that they are truly what they purport to be, and that they are not false, forged, fictitious, simulated, spurious, or counterfeit. Baldwin v. Van Deusen, 37 N. Y. 492; Smelt-zer v. white, 92 U. 8. 392, 23 L.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. A general class or dlvision, comprising several species. In toto jure generi per speciem derogatnr, et illud potisaimum habetur quod ad speciem directum eat, throughout the law, the species takes from the genus, and that is most particularly regarded which refers to the species. Dig. 50, 17, 80.

A warrant ordering a technology company to identify all devices located within a defined geographic area during a specified time period; raises Fourth Amendment third-party doctrine and particularity concerns.

This refers to the five regions that the world is divided into—Africa, East Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, Near East and South Asia, and the former Soviet Union and Eastern Europe—for the initial admission of refugees to the United States.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An English gold coin, valne 6s. 8d.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old New York law. A conrt messenger or constable. o’Cal-iaghan, New Neth. 322.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. Greve, reve, or reeve; a ministerial oflicer of high antiq-ulty in England; answering to the grave or graf (grafio) of the early continental nations. The term was applied to various grades of officers, from the seitre-gerefa, shirc-grefe, or shire-rere, who had charge of the county, (and whose title aud office have been perpetuated in the modern “sheriff,”) down to the tun-gerefa, or town-reeve, and lower. Burrill.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Bearing. Gerens datum, bear-lug date. l’Ld. Raym. 336; Hob. 19.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Descended of the same stock, or from the same couple of ancestors; of the whole or full blood. Mackeld. Rom.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. A sprout of the earth. A young tree, so called.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. offl-cers appointed to manage hospitals for the aged poor.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. An institution or hospital for taking care of the old. Cod. 1, 3, 46, 1; Calvin.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A name given to the process of dividing a stnte or other territory into the authorized civil or political divl-sions, but with such a geographical arrangement as to accomplish a sinister or unlawful purpose, as, for instance, to secure a majority for a given political party in districts where the result would be otherwise if they were divided according to obvious natural lines, or to arrange school districts so that children of certain religions or nationalities shall be brought within one district and those of a different religion or nationality in another district. State v. whitford, 54 wis. 150, 11 N. W. 424.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Finable; liable to be amerced at the discretion of the lord of a manor. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Expense; reward; compensation; wealth. It is also used for a flne or compensation for an offense. 2 Mon. Angl. 973.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. A guest A name given to a stranger on the second night of his entertainment in another’s house. Twa-night gest.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In medical jurisprudence. The time during which a female, who has conceived, carries the embryo or foetus in her uterus.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. Behavior or conduct.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. one who acts for another, or transacts another’s business. Calvin.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An ancient and obsolete writ resorted to when a person’s good behavior was impeached. Lamb. Eir. 1. 4, c. 14.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In Roman law. A deed or act; a thing done. Some writers affected to make a distinction between “gcstum” and “factum: But the best authorities pro-nouuced this subtile and indefensible.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Scotch law. Gaolers. 1 Pitc. Crim. Tr. pt. 2, p. 234.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon and old Eng-iish law. The giving of evidence.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. Deeds or charters; writings. 1 Reeve, Eng. Law, 10.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Roman law. A handwriting; that which was written with a person’s own hand. An obligation which a person wrote or subscribed with hls own hand; an acknowledgment of debt, as of money received, wlth a promise to repay.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Under the municipal organization of the state of New Jersey, each county has a board of officers, called by this name, composed of representatives from the cities and townships within its limits, and charged with administering the revenues of the county. They correspond to the “county commissioners” or "super-visors” in other states.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Hindu law. A fourth, a fourth part of the sum in litigation. The “Mahratta chout” is a fourth of the revenues exacted as tribute by the Mahrattas.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A gallows; the post on which malefactors are hanged, or on which their bodies are exposed. It differs from a common gallows, in that it consists of one perpendicular post, from the top of which proceeds one arm, except it be a double gibbet, which is formed in the shape of the Roman capital T. Enc. Loud.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. To lie. Gist en le bouche, it lies in the mouth.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A voluntary conveyance of land, or transfer of goods, from one person to another. made gratuitously, and not upon auy consideration of blood or money. 2 Bl. Comm. 440 ; 2 Steph. Comm. 102; 2 Kent, Comm. 437. And see Ingram v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The stream of water to a mill. Mon. Angl. tom. 3.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Swedish law. The right to dispose of a woman in marriage; or the person possessing such right,—her father, if living, or, if he be dead, the mother.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. A tax or tribute. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A gild mer-ebant, or merchant gild; a gild, corporation, or company of merchants. 10 Coke, 30.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Taxable, tributary, or contributory; liable to pay tax or tribute. Cowell; Blount.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. Members of a gild or decennary, oftener spelled "con-gildo.” Du Cange; Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. A cheat or deceiver. Applied in Britton to those who sold false or spurious things for good, as pewter for silver or laten for gold.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An Italian word, which sig-nifles the drawer of a bill. It is derived from “girare,” to draw.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon aud old English law. A measure of length, equal to one yard, de-iived from the girth or circumference of a man's body.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. Agistment; cattle taken in to graze at a certain price; also the money received for grazing cattle.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An agister; a person who takes cattle to graze.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. A pledge. Fred-gisle, a pledge of peace. Qislebert, an lllus-trious pledge.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In pleadlng. The essential ground or object of the actlon in point of law, withont which there would be no cause of action. Gould, Pl. c. 4, S 12; Hathaway v. Rlce, 19 Vt. 102.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To transfer or yleld to, or bestow upon, another, one of the operatlve words in deeds of conveyance of real property, importing at common law, a warranty or covenant for qulet enjoyment durlng the lifetime of the grantor. Mack v. Patchin, 29 How. Prac.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A donor; he who makes a glft.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Louisiana law. A phrase (translating the Fr. “Ration en payement”) which signifies the delivery and acceptance of real or personal property in satisfaction of a debt, Instead of a payment in money. See Civil Code La. art 2655.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A ceremony anciently performed In England by serjeants at law at the time of their appointment. The rlngs were inscribed with a motto, generally in Latin.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A little sword or dagger; a kind of sedge. Mat. Paris.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. A sword. An ancient emblem of defense. Hence the ancient earls or comites (the klng’s attendants, advisers, and associates in his government) were made by being girt with swords, (gladio succincti.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A sword, lance, or horseman's staff, one of tbe weapons allowed in a trlal by combat.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the clvll law. Acorns or nuts of the oak or other trees. In a larger sense, all fruits of trees.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The gathering of grain after reapers, or of grain left ungathered by reapers. Held not to be a right at common law. 1 H. Bl. 51.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A turf, sod, or clod of earth. The soil or ground; cultivated land in general. Church land, (solum et dos ecclesi.) Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Turfs dug out of the grouud. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Villein-socmen, who could not be removed from the land while they did the service due. Bract, c. 7; 1 Reeve, Eng. Law, 269.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Commissioners appointed to determine differences between scholars in a school or university and the townsmen of the place. Jacob.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil law. A husband’s sister. Dig. 38, 10, 4, 6.
