Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In practice. An error made by a judge in Instructing the jury npon the trial of a cause.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The Issue in a writ of right when the tenant in a writ of right pleads that his title is better than the demandant’s, he is said to join the mise on the mere right.

terms.term: Misera est servitus, ubi jus est vagum aut incertum
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: It is a miserable slavery where the law is vague or uncertain.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil law. The name of an Involuntary deposit, made under pressing necessity; as, for Instance, shipwreck, fire, or other inevitable calamity. Poth.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The name and first word of one of the penitential psalms, being that.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Mercy; a flne or amerciament; an arbltrary or discretionary amercement.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A misdeed or trespass. The doing what a party ought to do improperly. 1 Tidd, Pr. 4. The Improper performance of some act which a man may lawfully do. 3 Steph. Comm. 460.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An adverse event, ca-lam ity, or evil fortune, arising by accident, (or without the will or concurrence of him who suffers from it,) and not to be foreseen or guarded against by care or prudence. See 20 Q. B. Div. 816.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon and old English law. An unjust or irregular summoning to court; to speak unsteadlly iu court; to vary in one's plea. Cow.ell; Blount; Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To deposit in a place not afterwards recollected; to lose anything by forgetfulness of the piace where it was laid. Shehane v. State, 13 Tex. App. 535.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Delusive; calculated to lead astray or to lead into error. Instruc-tlous which are of such a nature as to be misunderstood by the Jury, or to give them a wrong impression, are said to be “mislead-ing.”
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Mistake in name; the giving an incorrect name to a person in a pleadlng, deed, or other Instrument.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Pleading incorrectly, or omitting anything in pleading which is es.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Reading a deed or other lnstrument to an llliterate or blind man (who is a party to lt) in a false or deceitful manner, so that he conceives a wrong idea of its tenor or contents. See 5 Coke, 19; 6 East, 309; IIallenbeck v. Dewitt, 2 Johns. (N. ¥.) 404.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The erroneous or incorrect recital of a matter of fact, elther in an agreement, deed, or pleading.
A false assertion of fact that induces a party to enter a contract. If the assertion is fraudulent or material and the other party justifiably relied on it, the contract is voidable.

Misrepresentation concerns a false or misleading representation that affects a party’s decision to agree. Analyze what was represented, why it was misleading, how it induced assent, and whether reliance was justified under the applicable rule.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Roman law. Gifts or liberalities, which the praetors and consuls were in the habit of throwing among the people. Inst. 2, 1, 45.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In maritime law. A vessel is so called when, computed from her known day of sailing, the time that has elapsed exceeds the average duration of similar voyages at the same season of the year. 2 Duer, Ins. 469.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil law. A sending or putting. Missio in bona, a putting the creditor in possession of the debtor’s property.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. writings passed between parties as evidence of a transaction. Bell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Some unintentional act, omission, or error arising from ignorance, surprise, imposition, or misplaced confidence. Code Ga. $ 3117; 1 Story, Eq. Jur. $ 110.

terms.term: Mistake about the bargain’s basic assumptions
terms.definition: Mistake concerns an erroneous belief about facts existing when the agreement is made. Relief depends on the significance of that assumption and who bears the risk that it is wrong.

In contract law, an erroneous belief about a fact existing when the contract was made. A mutual mistake about a basic assumption may make the contract voidable; a unilateral mistake generally does so only if the other party knew of or caused it, or enforcement would be unconscionable.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The proper style of the wife of an esquire or a gentleman in England.
An invalid trial, caused by fundamental error. When a mistrial is declared, the trial must start again with the selection of a new jury.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Abuse of an office or franchlse. 2 Bl. Comm. 153.
Those circumstances under which a crime is committed which, while not completely exonerating the person charged, at least reduces the penalty for the offense or the damages arising from the offense.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Alleviation; abatement or diminution of a penalty or punishment Imposed by law. “Mitigating circumstances” are such as do not constitute a justification or excuse of the offense in question, but which, in fairness and mercy, may be considered as extenuating or reducing the degree of moral culpability. See Heaton v. wright, 10 How. Prac.
The rule that an injured party cannot recover losses it could have avoided with reasonable effort after the breach, for example by making a substitute transaction.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): LaL The more favorable acceptation.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The more mildly one commands the better is he obeyed.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French law. The joint ownership of two neighbors in a wall, ditch, or hedge which separates their estates.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An abolished judicial writ addressed to the treasurer and chamberlain of the exchequer to search for and transmit the foot of a flne acknowledged before Justices in eyre into the common pleas. Reg. orig. 14.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. To put, to send, or to pass; as, mitter Vcstate, to pass the estate; mitter le droit, to pass a right These words are used to distinguish different kinds of re-leases.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. In old prae-tice. To put before; to present before a court; to produce in court.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In English law. A writ used in sending a record or its tenor from one court to another. Thus, where a nul tiei record is pleaded in one court to the record of another court of equal or superior jurisdiction, the tenor of the record is brought into chancery by a certiorari, (q. v.,) and thence sent by mittimus into the court where the action is. Tidd, Pr. 745.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Formed by admixture or commingling; partaking of the nature, character, or legal attributes of two or more dlstlnct kinds or classes.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The mixture or confusion of goods or chattels belonging severally to dlfferent owners, in such a way that they can uo longer be separated or distinguished; as where two measures of wine belonging to different persons are poured together into the same cask.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Timber; wood suitable tor building purposes.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. A general term including all those convocations of the lieges for violent and unlawful purposes, which are attended with In-Jury to the persons or property of the lieges, or terror and alarm to tbe neighborhood in which it takes place. The two phrases are usually placed together; but, nevertheless, they have distinct meanings, and are sometimes used separately in legal language, the word “mobbing” being peculiarly applicable to the unlawful assemblage nud violence of a number of persons, and that of “rioting” to the outrageous behavior of a single individual. Alls.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Movables; movable thiugs; otherwise called “res mobiles.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A kind of cloth made in England, mentioned in St. 23 Eliz. c. 9.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A pattern or representation of something to be made. A fac simile ot some.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In Roman law. The regula-tlon of justifiable defense. A term used to express that degree of force in defense of the person or property which a person might Bafely use, although it should occasion the death of the aggressor.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A writ founded on Magna Charta, which lies for him who is amerced in a court, not of record, for any transgression beyond the quality or quantity of the offense. It Ib addressed to the lord of the court, or his bailiff, com-mandlng Elm to take a moderate amerclament of the parties. New Nat Brev. 167; Fltzh. Nat.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In admiralty law. As applied to a steam-vessel, “such speed only is moderate as will permit the steamer reasonably and effectually to avold a collision by slackening speed, or by stopping and re-versing, within the distance at which an ap-proaching vessel can be seen.” The City of New York (C. C.) 35 Fed. 609; The Alliance (D. C.) 39 Fed. 480; The State of Alabama (D.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A chairman or president of an assembly. A person appointed to preside at a popular meeting. The presiding oflicer of town-meetings in New England is so called. See wheeler v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Engllsh law. A certaln duty pald for every tierce of wine.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The smallest circumstance may change the law.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A change; an alteration which introduces new elements into the details, or cancels some of them, but leaves the general purpose and effect of the subject-matter intact, wiley v. Corporation of BlufT-ton. 111 Ind. 152, 12 N. E. 165; State v. Tucker, 36 or. 291, 61 Pac. 894. 51 L.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To alter; to change in incl-dental or subordinate features.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. A measure. Speciflcal-ly, a Roman dry measure having a capncity of about 550 cubic Inches; but in medieval English law used as an approximate translation of the word “bushel.”

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in manner and form, words used in the old Latln forms of pleadings by way of traverse, and literally translated in the modern precedents, importing that the party traversing denies the allegation of the other party, not only in its general effect, but in the exact manner and form in which it is made. Steph. PL 189, 190.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In tbo oivil law. Manner; means; way.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Manner and agreement overrule the law.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The manner gives law to a gift.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. Movable. Biena moeblea, movable goods.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The secret killing of another; murder. 4 BL Comm. 194.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Hindu law. Separated; particularized; the subordinate divisions of a district in contradistinction to Builder or Sudder, which implies the chief seat of government wharton.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A system of native law prevailing among the Moham medans in India, and administered there by the British government.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French law. A transaction covering a fraudulent device to evade the laws agalnst usury.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A gold coin of Portugal, valued at twenty-seven English shllliugs.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The half of anything. Joint tenants are said to hold by moieties. Litt. 125; 3 C. B. 274, 283.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A grist; a certain quantity of corn sent to a mill to be ground.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. A possessory action calculated for continuing proprietors of lauded estates in the lawful possession of them till the point of right be determined against all who shall attempt to disturb thelr possession. It is chiefly used in questions of commonty or of controverted marches. Ersk.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The toll or multure paid for grinding corn at a mill. Jacob.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The laws of Dunvallo Molmutuis, a legendary or mythical king of the Britons, who is supposed te have begun his reign about 400 B. C. These law's were famous in the land till the Conquest Tomlins; Mozley & whltley.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. An ln-stant; an indivisible portion of time. Calvln.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A government in which the supreme power is vested in a single person. where a monarch is Invested with absolute power, the monarchy is termed “des-potlcwhere the supreme power is virtually in the laws, though the majesty of government and the administration are vested in a single person, it is a “limited” or “constitutional’ monarchy. It is hereditary where the regal power descends lmmediately from the possessor to the next helr by blood, as in England; or elective, as was formerly the case in Poland. lVharton.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A monastery; a church. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A book glvlng an account of monasteries, convents, and religious houses.

Municipal liability under § 1983 for constitutional violations caused by an official policy, widespread custom, or deliberate indifference to training needs; requires that the municipality's policy or custom be the moving force behind the violation.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A general, indefinite term for the measure and representative of value; currency; the circulating medium; cash.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): or MONEYEERS. Ministers of the mint; also bankers. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A dealer or seller. It is seldom or never used alone, or otherwise than after the name of any commodity, to express a seller of such commodity.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A memorial, superscription, or record.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In praotice. A monition is a formal order of the court commanding something to be done by tbe person to whom it is directed, and who is called the “person monished.” Thus, when money is decreed to be paid, a monition may he obtained commanding its payment. In ecclesiastical procedure, a monition is an order monishing or warning the party complained against to do or not to do a certain act “under pain of the law and contempt thereof.” A monition may also be appended to a sentence indicting a punishment for a past offense; in that case the monition forbids the repetition of tlie offense. Sweet.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Communications of warning and admonition sent from an ecclesiastical judge, upon information of scandal and abuses within the cognizance of his court.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A monarch who governs alone; an absolute governor.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tbe marriage of one wife only, or the state of such as are restrained to a single wife, webster.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A character or cipher composed of one or more letters interwoven, beiug an abbreviation of a name.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A special treatise upon a particular subject of limited range; a treatise or commentary upon a particular branch or division of a general subject.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In medical jurlspru-dence. Deraugement of a single faculty of the mind, or with regard to a particular sub-Ject, the other faculties being in regular exercise.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In commercial law. A privilege or pecullar advantage vested in one or more persons or companies, consisting in the exclusive right (or power) to carry on a partlcular buslness or trade, manufacture & partlcular. article, or control the sale of the whole supply of a partlcular commodity.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A prodigious birth; a human birth or offspring not havlng the shape of mankind, which cannot be heir to any land, albeit it be brought forth in marriage. Bract fol. 5; Co. Lltt 7, 8; 2 BL Comm. 246.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A box in which relics are kept; also a muster of soldiers. Cow'ell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. Forests or woods, white, New Recop. b. 2, tit 1, c. 6, I 1.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Public pawnbrok-lng establishments; institutions established by government, in some European countries, for lending small sums of money on pledgee of personal property. In France they are called “monts de piett.”
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Anything by which the memory of a person or an event is preserved or perpetuated. A tomb where a dead body has been deposited. Mead v. Case, 33 Barb.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): or MONUNG. In old English law. The district wlthin the jurisdictlon of a reeve, apparently so called from hls power to exerclse therein one of hls chief functions, viz., to exact (amaniah) all fines.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Norman law. Moneyage. A tax or tribute of one shilling on every hearth, payable to the duke every three years, in consideration that he should not alter the coln. Hale, Com.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Hlndu law. An agent or attorney.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Hlndu law. A wrltten authority constituting an agent; a power of attorney.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An officer in the Isle of Man, who summons the courts for the several sheadings. The office is similar to the English bailiff of a hundred.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A sum due by law or usage for mooring or fastening of ships to trees or posts at the shore, or to a wharf, wharf Case, 3 Bland (Md.) 373.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In maritime law. Anchor-ing or making fast to the shore or dock; the securing or confining a vessel in a particular station, as by cables and anchors or by a line or chaln run to the wharf. A vessel is “moored in safety,” wlthln the meaning of a policy of marine insurance, when she is thus moored to a wharf or dock, free from any immediate danger from any of the perils Insured against. See 1 Phil.
Not subject to a court ruling because the controversy has not actually arisen, or has ended.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A pack of dogs. Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The exercise of arguing questions of law or equity, raised for the purpose.
A case that began with standing may continue after a defendant stops the challenged conduct unless the defendant meets the demanding standard for voluntary-cessation mootness.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil lnw. Delay; default; neglect; culpable delay or default Calvin.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Delay is disapproved of in law.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Pertaining or relating to the conscience or moral sense or to the general principles of right conduct.

A crime of moral turpitude is one demonstrating baseness, vileness, or depravity in the private and social duties which a man owes to his fellow men, or to society in general, contrary to the accepted and customary rule of right and duty between man and man; conviction of a crime of moral turpitude may lead to disqualification from office, loss of licensed employment and deportation of immigrants.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. He delays in law. The phrase describes the action of.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): otherwise called “Herra-hutters” or “United Brethren.” A sect of Christians whose social polity is particular and conspicuous. It sprung up in Moravia and Bohemia, on the opening of that reforma-tlon whlch stripped the chair of St. Peter of so many votaries, and gave birth to so many denominations of Christians. They give evidence on tbeir solemn affirmation. 2 Steph.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in the clv-11 law. A sickness which rendered a man Incapable of attendlng to business.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in old pleading. In husband-llke manner. Townsh. PL 198.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Thls phrase, Inserted in a conveyance of land lmmediately after the statement of the quantity of land conveyed, means that such statement is not to be taken as a warranty of the quantity, but only an approximate estimate, and that the tract or parcel described is to pass, without regard to ah excess or deficiency in the quantity it actually contains. See Brawley v. U.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Anglo-Dutch. In old New York law. A measure of land, equal te about two acres.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A place where the bodies of persons found dead are kept for a limited time and exposed to view, to the end that their friends may identify them.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A social and rellglous system prevailing in the territory of Utah, a distinctive feature of which is the practlce of polygamy. These plural marriages are not recognized by law, hut are indictable offenses under the statutes of the Unlted States and of Utah.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Death is denominated the extreme penalty.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): ELLUS, TER-RJE. In old English law. A small parcel or bit bf land.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French law. Civil death, as upon conviction for felony. It was nominally abollshed by a law of the 31st of May, 1854, but something very similar to it, in effect at least, still remains. Thus, the property of the condemned, possessed by him at the date of his conviction, goes and belongs to his successors, (hdritiers,) as in case of an lntestacy; and his future acquired property goes to the state by right of Its prerogative, (par droit de ddshdrence,) but the state may, as a matter of grace, make it over in whole or in part to the widow and children.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Thls word in its ordi' nary sense, never means violent death, but death arising from natural causes. Law rence v. Aherdein, 5 Barn. & Ald. 110.

A mortgage involves the transfer of an interest in land as security for a loan or other obligation. It is the most common method of financing real estate transactions. The mortgagor is the party transferring the interest in land. The mortgagee (usually a financial institution) is the provider of the loan or other interest given in exchange for the security interest.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): He that takes or receives a mortgage.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Sax. Murder, answering exactly to the French “assassinat" or “muertre de ffuct-apens.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. A term nearly synonymous with “mortmain." Bell. Lands are said to be mortified for a charitable purpose.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat By reason of death; in contemplation of death. Thus used in the phrase “Donatio mortis causa," (q. v.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A term applied to denote the alienation of lands or tenements to any corporation, sole or aggregate, ecclesiastical or temporal. These purchases havlng been chiefly made hy rellglous houses, in consequence of which lands became perpetually inherent in one dead hand, this has occasioned the general appellation of "mortmain" to be applled to such alienations. 2 BL Comm. 268; Co. Lltt 2b; Perln v. Carey, 24 How. 495, 16 L.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In ecclesiastical law. burial-place. A kind of ecclesiastical heriot, being a customary gift of the second best living animal belonging to the deceased, claimed by and due to the ninister in many parishes, on the death of his parishioners, whether buried in the church-yard or not 2 Bl. Comm. 425. Ayrton v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Tables for estimating the probable duration of the life of a party at a given age. Gallagher v. Mar ket St. Ry.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A dead pledge; a mortgage, (q. v,;) a pledge where the profits.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat Dead. So in sheriff's return, mortwu est, be is dead.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: To be dead born is not to be born.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. Strayed goods; estrays, white, New Recop. b. 2, tit 2, c. 6.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Sax. A meeting; an assembly. Used in composition, as burgmote, folkmote, etc.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A customary servlce or payment at the mote or court of the lord, from which some were exempted by charter or privilege. Cowell.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A woman who has borne a child; a female parent; correlative to “son" or “daughter.” The term may also include a woman who is pregnant See Howard v. People, 185 111. 552, 57 N. E. 441; Latshaw v. State, 156 Ind. 194, 59 N.
A request by a litigant to a judge for a decision on an issue relating to the case.
The pleading filed in cases seeking monetary damages.
A motion under Rule 59 asking the court to set aside a verdict and retry the case because of errors, misconduct, newly discovered evidence, or a verdict against the great weight of the evidence.

A pretrial motion requesting the court to prohibit the other side from presenting, or even referring to, evidence on matters said to be so highly prejudicial that no steps taken by the judge can prevent the jury from being unduly influenced.

A pre-answer motion under Rule 12(b) asking the court to end the case for a listed defect such as lack of jurisdiction, improper venue, insufficient service, or failure to state a claim. Some defenses are waived if not raised in the first motion or answer (Rule 12(h)).

terms.term: Motion to lift the automatic stay
terms.definition: A request by a creditor to allow the creditor to take action against the debtor or the debtor's property that would otherwise be prohibited by the automatic stay.
An oral or written request to the judge to dismiss the case completely because the prosecution has not proven the charges or because of some other legal defect in the prosecution’s case.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The inducement, cause, or reason why a thing is done. An act legal in itself, and which violates no right, is not actionable on account of the motive which actuated lt. Chatfield v. wilson, 5 Am. Law Reg.
A party’s personal reason for contracting can differ from the performance or promise that serves as the agreed exchange.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. of his own motion. The commencing words of a certain kind of papal rescript.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The dress or apparel worn by mourners at a funeral and'for a time afterwards. Also the expenses paid for such apparel.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): By statute In some states, the mouth of a river or creek, which empties into another river or creek, is defined as the point where the middle of the channel of each Intersects the other. Pol. Code Cal. 1903, S 3908; Rev. St.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): That which can be changed in place, as movable property; or in time, aa movable feasts or terms of court See wood v. George, 6 Dana (Ky.) 343; Strong v. white, 19 Conn. 245; Goddard v. winchell. 86 Iowa, 71, 52 N. W. 1124, 17 L. R.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Things movable; movable or personal chattels, which may be annexed to or attendant on the person of the owner, and carried about with him from one part of the world to another. 2 Bl. Comm. 387. Movables consist—First, ot Inanimate things, as goods, plate, money, jewels, implemeuts of war, garments, and the like, or vegetable productions, as the fruit or other parts of a plant when severed from the body of lt, or the whole plant itself when severed from the ground; secondly, of anlmals, whlch have in themselves a principle and power of motion. 2 Steph. Comm. 67.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To make an application to a court for a rule or order.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): one who moves; one who makes a motion before a court; the applicant for a rule or order.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Making a motion on a day which is not motlon day, in virtue of having argued a special case; used in the exchequer after it became obsolete in the queen’s bench, wharton.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Saxon law. A recompense or satisfaction for the slaying or murder of a kinsman. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Famous; great; noted; as z2?l-mere, all famous. Gibs. Camd.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. Movables; all sorts of personal property, white, New Recop. b. 1, tlt. 3, c. 1, § 2.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. The offense of setting fire to a muir or moor. 1 Brown, Ch. 78, 116.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A mulatto is defined to be “a person that is the offspring of a negress by a white man, or of a white woman by a negro.” Thurman v. State, 18 Ala. 276.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A penalty or punishment 1m-posed on a person guilty of some ofTense. tort, or mlsdemeanor, usually a pecuniary fine or condemnation in damages. See Cook v. Mar-shall County, 119 Iowa, 384, 93 N. W. 372, 104 Am.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. (1) A woman; (2) a virgin; (3) a wife; (4) a legitimate child.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. when man has a bastard son, and afterwards marries the mother, and by her has also a legitimate son, the elder son is bastard cignd, and the younger son is mulier puisnd.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. The state or conditlon of a mulier, or lawful issue. Co. Litt 352b.

terms.term: Multa conceduntur per obliquum quae non conceduntur de directo
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Many things are conceded indirectly which are not allowed directly. 6 co. 47.

terms.term: Multa multo exercitatione facilius quam regulis percipies
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: You will perceive many things more easily by practice than by rules.

terms.term: Multa transeunt cum universitate quae non per se transeunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Many things pass as a whole which would not pass separately.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Many men know many things, no one knows everything.
The transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1407 of civil actions pending in different districts that share common questions of fact to a single district for coordinated pretrial proceedings.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In equity pleading. The fault of improperly joining In one hill distinct and independent matters, and thereby confounding them; as, for example, the uniting in one bill of several matters perfectly distinct and unconnected against one defendant, or the demand of several matters of a distinct and independent nature against several defendants, in the same bill. Story, Eq. PL S 271.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Divided Into many or several parts.

terms.term: Multiple claims against an opposing party
terms.definition: Claim joinder allows a party to assert more than one claim against an existing opposing party. Federal Rule 18 provides broad procedural permission even when claims differ in subject or legal theory.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. Double distress; a name given to an action, corresponding to proceedings by way of in-terpleader, which may be bronght by a person in possession of goods claimed by different persons pretending a right thereto, calling the claimants and all others to settle thelr clalms, so that the party who sues may he liable only “in once and single payment BelL.

terms.term: Multiplex et indistinctum parit confusionem; et questiones quo simpliciores, eo lucidiores
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Multiplicity and indistinctness produce confusion; the more simple questions are the more lucid.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The increase of punishment shouldbe in proportion to the increase of crime.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A state of being many. That quality of a pleading which lnvolves a variety of matters or particulars; undue variety. 2 Saund. 410. A multiply-ing or increasing. Story.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): An assemblage of many people. According to Coke it is not a word of very precise meaning; for some authorities hold that there must be at least ten persons to make a multitude, while others maintain that no definite number is fixed by law. Co. Litt. 257.

terms.term: Multitudo errantium non parit errori patrocinium
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The multitude of those who err is no excuse for error.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: A multitude of ignorant practitioners destroys a court.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old records. A wether sheep.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch law. Thequan-tlty of grain or meal payable to the proprietor of a mill, or to the multurer, his tacks-man, for manufacturing the corns. Ersk. Inst 2, 9, 19.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In medical jurisprudence. A term applied to the complete drying up of the body. It is the result « burial in a dry, hot soil, or the exposure of the body to a continuously cold and dry at-mosphere. 15 Amer. & Eng. Enc.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Antic diversions in the Christmas holidays, suppressed In Queen Anne’s time.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. Peace; wheuce mundbryc, a breach of the peace.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old French law. A tril ute paid by a church or monastery to their seignorlal avouds and vidames, as the price of protecting them. Steph. Lect 236.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the early ages of the feudal law, this was the name given to the grants of land made by a king or chieftain to his followers, which were held by no certain tenure, but merely at the will of the lord. Afterwards they became life-es-tates, and then hereditary, and were called first “benefices.” and then “feuds.” See wright, Ten. 19.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in Roman law. A provincial person; a countryman. This was the designation of one born in the provinces or in a city politically connected with Rome, and who, having become a Roman citizen, was entitled to hold any offices at Rome except some of the highest. In the provinces the term seems to have been applied to the freemen of any city who were eligible to the munlclpal offices.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): “Municipal” signifies that whlch belongs to a corporation or a city. The term Includes the rules or laws by which a particular district, communlty, or nation is governed. It may also mean local, particular, Independent Horton ▼. Mobile School Com’rs, 43 Ala. 598.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A pub-iic corporation, created by government for political purposes, and having subordinate and local powers of legislation; e. g., a county, town, city, etc. 2 Kent, Comm. 275.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A munlclpal corpo ration; a city, town, borough, or incbrporat-ed village. Also the body of officers, taken collectively, belonglng to a city.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Roman law. A foreign town to which the freedom of the city of Rome was granted, and whose inhabitants had the privilege of enjoying oflices and honors there; a free town. Adams, Rom. Ant 47, 77.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): E, or MUNIMENT-ROOM. A house or room of strength, in cathedrals, collegiate churches, castles, col-leges, public bulldings, etc., purposely made for keeping deeds, charters, writings, etc.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The instruments of writing and written evidences which the owner of lands, possesslons, or Inheritances has, t y which he is enabled to defend the title of his estate. Termes de la Ley; 3 Inst. 170.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In interua-tlonal law and United States statutes, this tenn Includes not only ordnance, ammunl-tion, and other material directly useful lo the conduct of a war, but also whatever may contribute to its successful maintenance.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat A gift; an office; a beu-eflce or feud. A gladiatorial show or spec-tacie. Calvin.; Du Cange.

The unlawful killing of a human being with malice aforethought, either express or implied; a special form of murder is the "felony murder" where the defendant unintentionally kills or causes to be killed another person in the commission or attempted commission of a felony; Virginia has various "degrees" of murder, each of which has various punishments.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. The killing of a man in a secret manner.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Tlie service of work and labor done by lnhabitants and adjotnlng tenants in bulldlug or repairing the walls of a clty or castle; their personal service was commuted into murage, (q. v.) Cowell.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old Scotch law. Mur-ther or murder. Skene.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A building or institution for the cultivation of science or the exhibition of curiosities or works of art.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A moss or marsh ground, or a place where sedges grow; a place overrun with moss. Cowell.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To assemble together troops and their arms, whether for inspection, drill, or service in the field. To take recruits into the service in the army and inscribe their names on the muster-roll or official record. See Tyler v. Pomeroy, 8 Allen (Mass.) 498.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A name given to the Issue of an Indian and a negro. Miller v. Dawson, Dud. (S.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A kennel of hounds; one of the mortuaries to which the crown was entitled st a bishop’s or abbot’s decease. 2 Bl. Comm. 426.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French law. This term is synonymous with “change,” and is especially applied to designate the change which takes place in the property of a thing in its transmission from one person to another. Mutation, therefore, happens when the owner of the thiug sells, exchanges, or gives it. Merl.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In practice. An amendment allowed to a libel, hy which there is an alteration of the substance of the libel, as by propounding a new cause of action, pr asking oue thing instead of another. Dunl. Adm.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. with the necessary changes in points of detail.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Speechless; dumb; that cannot or will not speak. In English crlminal law, a prisoner is sald to stand, mute when, heing arraigned for treason or felony, he either makes no answer at all, or answers foreign to the purpose or with such matter as is not allowable, and will not auswer otherwise, or, upon having pleaded not guilty, refuses to put himself upon the country. 4 Bl. Comm. 324.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): As applied to written documents, such as wills, court records, and the like, this term means renderlng the document imperfect by the subtraction from it of some essential part, as, by cutting, tear.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Insubordinate; disposed to mutiny; tendlng to incite or encourage mutiny.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In crlminal law. An insurrection of soldiers or seamen against the au-thorlty of their commanders; a sedition or revolt in the army or navy. See The St^-cey Clarke (D. C.) 54 Fed. 533; McCargo v.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Interchangeable; reciprocal; each acting in return or correspondence to the other; given and received; spoken of an engagement or relation in which like duties aud obligations are exchanged.
The agreement of both parties to the same terms, judged objectively by what the parties said and did rather than by their private intentions. Mutual assent is usually shown by offer and acceptance.

A shared erroneous belief about a basic assumption on which the contract was made that materially affects the exchange. The adversely affected party may avoid the contract unless it bore the risk of the mistake.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Reciprocation; interchange. An acting by each of two partles; an acting in return.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The persou who leuds chattels in the contract of mutuum, (q. v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To borrow; mutuatus, a borrowing. 2 Arch. Pr. 25.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A person who borrows personal chattels to be consumed by him and returned to the lender in kind and quau-tlty; the borrower in a contract of mutuum.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In civll and old English law. Dumb and deaf.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the law of bailments. A loan for consumption; a loan of chattels, upon an agreement that the borrower may consume them, returning to the lender an equivalent in kind and quantity. Story, Bailm.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Monastic habitation; perhaps the part of a monastery set apart fo.r purposes of hospitality, or as a sanctuary for criminals. Anc. Inst Eng.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A trade, art, or occupation. 2 Inst 668. Masters frequently bind themselves in the indentures with their appren-tices to teach them their art, trade, and mystery. State v. Bishop, 15 Me. 122; Bar-ger v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The state of a nation which takes no part between two or more other nations at war. U. S. v. The Three Friends, 166 U.

terms.term: N O N intromittendo, quando breve prsscipe in capite sub-dole impetratur
terms.definition: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A writ addressed to the justices of the bench, or in eyre, com-raanding them not to give one who, under color of entitling tbe king to land, etc., as holding of him in capite, had deceitfully obtained the writ called “priccipe in capite," any benefit thereof, but to put him to bis writ of right Reg. orig. 4.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): ne can grant or convey wbat he does not own. Seymour v. Canandaigua & N. F.
Section 5-1103 prevents specified written, signed modifications or discharges from failing merely for lack of consideration.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Sax. The attaching or taking of movable goods and chattels, called “vif” or “mort” according as the chattels were living or dead. Termes de la Ley.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): . originally the governor of a province nnder the Mogul government of Hlndostan, whence it became a mere title of any man of high rank, upon whom it was conferred without any office being attached to it. wils. Indian Gloss.
This is an acronym for the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act.
This is the North American Industry Classification System Code: A character string that refers to an industry classification within the North American Industry Classification System.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. A villein; a born slave; a bondwoman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A lineal measure of two inches and a quarter.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): As a term of jurisprudence, this word is equivalent to hare, wanting in necessary conditions, lncomplete, as a naked contract, (niifluni pactum,) i. e., a contract de-void of consideration, and therefore Invalid; or simple, unilateral, comprising hut a single element, as a naked authority, i. c., one w’hich is not coupled with any interest in the agent, but subsists for the benefit of the principal alone.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Lat in old records. To take, seize, or distrain.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Lat. In old English and Scotch law. A distraining or taking of a distress; an impounding.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The designation of an individual person, or of a firm or corporation. In law a man cannot have more than one Christian name. Rex v. Newman, 1 Ld.

terms.term: Named-party joinder and representative class actions
terms.definition: Joinder combines claims of persons who are individually parties. A class action allows named representatives to litigate for absentees after satisfying the requirements for legitimate representation.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Lat in old English law. A taking; a dlstress. Spelman.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A celebrated law for the security of Protestants, made by Henry IV. of France, and revoked by Louis XIV., october 2, 1685.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A common abbreviation of “nar-ratio," (q. v.) A declaration in au action. Jacob.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat one of the common law names for a plaintiff’s count or declaration, as being a narrative of the facts on which he relies.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Scotch conveyancing. That part of a deed which describes the grantor, and person in whose favor the deed is granted, and states the cause (consideration) of granting. BelL.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A countor; a pleader who draws nam. Serviens narrator, a serjeant at law. Fleta, 1. 2, c. 37.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Those seas which run between two coasts not far apart. The term is sometimes applied to the English channel, wharton.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. That shall hereafter be born. A term used in marriage settlements to designate the future issue of the marriage, as distinguished from “natus" a child already horn.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The state and condition of a man acquired by birth.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Born and to be born. All heirs, near and remote.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old records. A native place. Coweli.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A people, or aggregation of men, existing in the form of an organized jural society, inhabiting a distinct portion of the earth, speaking the same language, using the same customs, possessing historic contin-uity, and distinguished from other like groups by their racial origin and characteristics, and generally, but not necessarily, living under the same government and sovereignty. See Montoya v. U. S., 180 U.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Pertaiuing or relating to a nation as a whole; commonly applied in American law to institutions, laws, or affairs of the United States or its government, as opposed to those of the several states. —National bank. A bank incorporated and doing business under the laws of tbe United States, as distinguished from a state hank, which derives its powers from the authority of a particular state.—National ourrency. Notes issued by national banks, and by the United States government.—National debt. The money owing by government to some of the public, the interest of which is paid out of the taxes raised by the whole of the public.—National domain.
A person who, though not a citizen of the United States, owes permanent allegiance to the United States (for example, persons born in American Samoa or Swains Island).

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): That quality or character which arises from the fact of a person’s belonging to a nation or state. Nationality determines the political status ot the indi-vldual, especially with reference to allegiance; while domicile determlnes his civil status. Nationality arises either by birth or by naturalization. According to Savigny, “nationality" is also used as opposed to “ter-ritoriality," for the purpose of distinguishing the case of a nation having no national territory; e. g., the Jews. 8 Sav.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish and Mexican law. Nationalization. “The na-tlonalization of property is an act which denotes that it has become that of the nation by some process of law, whereby private individuals or corporations have been for speci-fled reasons deprived thereof.” Hall, Mex. Law, 8 749.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A natural-born subject or citl-zen; a denizen by blrth; one who owes his domicile or citizenship to the fact of his birth within the country referred to. The term may also include one born abroad, if his parents were then citizens of the country, and not permanently residing in foreign parts. See U. S. v. wong Kim Ark, 169 U.

As a nonimmigrant class of admission, this is an noncitizen coming temporarily to the United States as a member of the armed forces or as a civilian employed by the armed forces on assignment with a foreign government signatory to NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization), and the noncitizen’s spouse and unmarried minor (or dependent) children.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in old English law, a native; specifically, one born iuto a condition of servitude; a born serf or villein. —Nativa. A niefe or female villein. So called because for the most part bond by nativity. Co.

terms.term: Natura appetit perfectum, ita et lex
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Nature aspires to perfection, and so does the law.

terms.term: Natura no facit vacuum, nec lex supervacuum
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Nature makes no vacuum, the law no supervacuum.

terms.term: Natura non facit saltum, ita nec lex
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Nature makes no leap, nor does the law.

terms.term: Naturae vis maxima, natura bis maxima
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: The force of nature is greatest; nature is doubly great.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The juristic meanlng of this term does not differ from the vernacular, except in the cases where it is used in op.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A rule of couduct arising out of the natural relations of human beings, established by the Creator, tfnd existing prior to any posltlve precept webster. The foundation of thls law is placed by the best writers in the will of God, discovered by right reason, and aided by divine revela-tion; and its principles, when applicable, apply with equal obligation to Individuals and to nations. 1 Kent, Comm. 2, note; ld. 4, note.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Spanish law. The state, of a natural-born subject white, New Recop. b. 1, tit. 5, c. 2.
The manner in which a person not born in the United States voluntarily becomes a U.S. citizen.
We issue this certificate to a person who becomes a U.S. citizen through the naturalization process after their 18th birthday.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To confer citizeushlp upou an alien; to make a foreigner the same, in respect to rights and privileges, as if he were a native citizen or subject.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Damages which “naturally” arise from a breach of. contract are such as arise in the usual course of things, from the breach itself, or such as may reasonably be supposed to have been contem-piated by tbe parties when making the contract as the probable result of the breach. Mitchell v. Clarke, 71 Cal. 164, 11 Pac. 882, 60 Am. Rep. 529.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Born, as distinguished from nasciturus, about to be born. Ante natus, one born before a particular person or event, e. g.. before tbe death of his father, before a political revolution, etc. Post natus, one born after a particular person or event.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil law. The master or owner of a merchant vessel. Calvin.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In French maritime law. 8hlpwreck. “The violent agitation of the waves, the impetuous force of the winds, storm, or lightning, may swallow up the ves.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old practice. Bad; defec-, tive. “The bar is naught." 1 Leon. 77. “The avowry is naught." 5 Mod. 73.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The freight of passengers-in a ship. Johnson; webster.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. The freight or fare paid for the transportation of cargo or passengers over the sea in a vessel. This is a Latinized form of a Greek word.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in the civil and maritlme law. A sailor; one who works a ship. Calvin.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Pertaining to ships or to the art of navigation or the business of carriage by sea.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In the civil law. Nautical or maritime interest; an extraordinary rate of Interest agreed to be paid for the loan of money on the hazard of a voyage; corresponding to interest on contracts of bottomry or respondentia in English and American maritime law. See Mackeld.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In old English law. A duty on certain tenants to carry thelr lord’s goods in a ship.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Appertaining to the navy, (q. v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. The . master or commander of a ship; the captain ef a man-of-war.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In the civil law. The master or captain of a ship. Galvin.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Capable of being navigated; that may be navigated or passed over in ships or vessels. But the term is generally understood in a more restricted sense, viz., subject to the ebb and flow of the tide.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): The act or the science or the buslness of traversing the sea or other waters In ships or vessels. Pollock v. Cleve-land Ship Building Co., 56 ohio St. 655, 47 N. E. 582; The Silvia, 171 U.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Fr. In French law. A ship. Emerig.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): To conduct vessels through navigable waters; to use the waters as a means of communication. Ryan v. Hook, 34 Hun (N. Y.) 185.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A fleet of ships; the aggregate of vessels of war belonging to an independent nation. In a broader sense, and as equlvalent to “naval forces," the entire corps of officers and men enlisted in the naval service and who man the pnblic ships of war, Including in this sense, in the United States, the officers and men of the Marine Corps. See wilkes v. Dinsman, 7 How. 124, 12 L.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): A sum paid to government as an acknowledgment for a grant of lands, or any publlc office. Enc. Lond.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In Hindu law. Composer, ar-ranger, adjuster. The first officer of a province, and minister of the department of criminal justice.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat in the civU law. Marriageable; one who is of a proper age to be married.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In ecclesiastical law. The name of a prohibitory writ, directed to the bishop, at the request of the plaintiff or defendant, where a quare impedit is pending, when either party fears that the bishop will admit the other’s clerk pending the suit between them. Fitzh.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. (Does or did not disturb.) In English practice. The general issue or general plea in quare impedit. 8 Steph.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In English practice. A writ which issues to restrain a person from leaving the kingdom. It was formerly used for political purposes, but is now only resorted to in equity when the defendant is about to leave the kingdom; it is only In cases where the intention of the party to leave can be shown that the writ is granted.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In American practice. A writ similar to that of ne exeat regno, (q. v..) avallable to the plaintiff in a civil suit, under some circumstances, when the defendant is about to leave the state. See Dean v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. In old English practice. A prohibitory writ, com.

terms.definition: Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. That nothing shall be done (put or erected) in a public place or way. The title of an interdict in the Roman law. Dig. 43, 8.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Fr. He did not deliver. A plea in detinue, denying the delivery to the defendant of the thing sued for.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. That it be not received. A caveat or warning given to a law ofiicer, by a party in a cause, not to receive the next proceedings of his opponent. 1 Sell. Pr. 8.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): L. Lat. The statute 35 Edw. I. { 2, prohibiting rectors, i. e., parsons, from cutting down the trees in church-yards.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): In pleading. The statement in apt and appropriate words of all the necessary facts, and no more. Lawes, Pl. 62.

This is a relative term, and its meaning will contract or expand according to the situation and social condition of the person referred to. Megraw v. woods, 93 Mo. App. 647, 67 S.

terms.term: Necessarium est quod non potest aliter se habere
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: That is necessity which cannot be dispensed with.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat Necessary; nn-a void able; Indispensable; not admitting of choice or the action of the will; needful.

Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): As used in jurisprudence^ the word "necessary" does not always import an absolute physical necessity, so strong that one thing, to wbich another may be termed "necessary," cannot exist without that other. It frequently imports no more than that one thing is convenient or useful or esseutial to another. To employ the means necessary to an end is generally understood as employing any means calculated to produce the end, and not as being confined to those single means without which the end would be entirely un-attainable. McCulloch v.
Black's Law Dictionary (2nd ed. 1910): Lat. Necessity; a force, power, or influence which compels one to act agninst hls will. Calvin.

terms.term: Necessitas est lex temporis et loci
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Necessity is the law of a particular time and place. 8 Co. 69; H.

terms.term: Necessitas facit licitum quod alias non est licitum
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Necessity makes that lawful which otherwise is unlawful.

terms.term: Necessitas inducit privililegium quoad jura privata
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Necessity gives a preference with regard to private rights.

terms.term: Necessitas publica major est quam private
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Public necessity is greater than private.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Necessity defends what it compels.

Negligence is the failure to behave with the level of care that a reasonable person would have exercised under the same circumstances. Either a person’s actions or omissions of actions can be found negligent. The omission of actions is considered negligent only when the person had a duty to act (e.g., a duty to help someone because of one’s own previous conduct). Negligence is a foundational concept of tort law.

terms.term: Nemo allegans suam turpitudinem, audiendus est

terms.term: Nemo bis punitur por eodem delicto
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one can be punished twice for the same crime or misdemeanor.

terms.term: Nemo cogitur rem suam vendere, etiam justo pretio
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to sell his property, even for a just price.

terms.term: Nemo contra factum suum venire potest
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No man can contradict his own deed.

terms.term: Nemo damnum facit, nisi qui id fecit quod facere jus non habet
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is considered as committing damages, unless he is doing what he has no right to do.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one can give who does not possess.

terms.term: Nemo de domo sua extrahi debet
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: A citizen cannot be taken by force from his house to be conducted before a judge or to prison.

terms.term: Nemo debet esse judex in propria causa
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one should be judge in his own cause.

terms.term: Nemo debet ex aliena jactura lucrari
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one ought to gain by another's loss.

terms.term: Nemo debet immiscere se rei alienae ad se nihil pertinenti
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one should interfere in what no way concerns him.

terms.term: Nemo debet rem suam sine facto aut defectu suo amittere
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one should lose his property without his act or negligence.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No man ought to be burdened in consequence of another's act.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No man is bound for the advice he gives.

terms.term: Nemo ex suo delicto melioroem suam conditionem facere potest
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one can improve his condition by a crime.

terms.term: Nemo in propria causa testis ese debet

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No man can renounce the country in which he was born, nor abjure the obligation of his allegiance.

terms.term: Nemo plus juris ad alienum transfere potest, quam ispe habent
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: One cannot transfer to another a right which he has not.

terms.term: Nemo potest contra recordum verificare per patriam
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one can verify by the country against a record.

terms.term: Nemo potest esse tenes et dominus
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No man can be at the same time tenant and landlord of the same tenement.

terms.term: Nemo potest facere per alium quod per se non potest
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one can do that by another which he cannot do by himself.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: One is not present unless he understands.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is presumed to trifle at the point of death.

terms.term: Nemo praesumitur alienam posteritatem suae praetulisse
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is presumed to have preferred another's posterity to his own.

terms.term: Nemo praesumitur esse immemor suae aeternae salutis, et maxime in articulo mortis
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No man is presumed to be forgetful of his eternal welfare, and particularly at the point of death.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is punished unless for some wrong, act or default.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to an impossibility.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to arm his adversary.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to inform about a thing he knows not, but he who gives information is bound to know what he says.

terms.term: Nemo tenetur jurare in suam turpitudinem
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to testify to his own baseness.

terms.term: Nemo tenetur seipsam infortunis et periculis exponere
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to expose himself to misfortune and dangers.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: No one is bound to accuse himself.

terms.term: Nemo videtur fraudare eos qui sciunt, et consentiunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: One cannot complain of having been deceived when he knew the fact and gave his consent.

terms.term: Nemo, qui condemnare potest, absolvere non potest
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who may condemn may acquit.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Words spoken to one end, ought not to be perverted to another.

terms.term: Quae cohaerent personae a persona separari nequeunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Things which belong to the person ought not to be separated from the person.

terms.term: Quae communi legi derogant stricte interpretantur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Laws which derogate from the common law ought to be strictly construed.

terms.term: Quae contra rationem juris introducta sunt, non debent trahi in consequentiam
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Things introduced contrary to the reason of the law, ought not to be drawn into precedents.

terms.term: Quae dubitationis causa tollendae inseruntur communem legem non laedunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Whatever is inserted for the purpose of removing doubt, does not hurt or affect the common law.

terms.term: Quae in auria acta sunt rite agi praesummuntur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Whatever is done in court is presumed to be rightly done.

terms.term: Quae in partes dividi nequeunt solida, a singulis praestantur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Things which cannot be divided into parts are rendered entire severally.

terms.term: Quae incontinenti vel certo fiunt inesse videntur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Whatever is done directly and certainly, appears already in existence.

terms.term: Quae inter alios acta sunt nemini nocere debent, sed prodesse possunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Transactions between strangers may benefit, but cannot injure, persons who are parties to them.

terms.term: Quae malasunt inchoata in principio vex bono peragantur exitu
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Things bad in the commencement seldom end well.

terms.term: Quae non valeant singula, juncta juvant
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Things which do not avail singly, when united have an effect.

terms.term: Quae praeter consuetudinem et morem majorum fiunt, neque placent, necque recta videntur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: What is done contrary to the custom of our ancestors, neither pleases nor appears right.

terms.term: Quae rerum natura prohibentur, nulla lege confirmata sunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Whatis prohibited in the nature of things, cannot be confirmed by law.

terms.term: Quaecumque intra rationem legis inveniuntur, intra legem ipsam esse judicantur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Whatever appears within the reason of the law, ought to be considered within the law itself.

terms.term: Quaelibet concessio fortissime contra donatorem interpretanda est
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Every grant is to be taken most strongly against the grantor.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Every jurisdiction has its bounds.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Inquire into them, is the way to know what things are really true.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Although, in itself, a thing may not be had, yet, if it holds out a bad example, it is not to be done.

terms.term: Quando abest provisio partis, adest provisio legis
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: A defect in the provision of the party is supplied by a provision of the law.

terms.term: Quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When anything is prohibited directly, it is prohibited indirectly.

terms.term: Quando duo juro concurrunt in und persona, aequum est ac si essent in diversis
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When two rights concur in one person, it is the same as if they were in two separate persons.

terms.term: Quando lex aliquid alicui concedit, concedere videtur id sine quo res ipsa esse non potest
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When the law gives anything, it gives the means of obtaining it.

terms.term: Quando lex aliquid alicui concedit, omnia incidentia tacite conceduntur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When the law gives anything, it gives tacitly what is incident to it.

terms.term: Quando lex est specialis, ratio autem generalis, generaliter lex est intelligenda
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When the law is special, but its reason is general, the law is to be understood generally. 2 co.

terms.term: Quando licet id quod majus, videtur licere id quod minus
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When the greate is allowed, the less seems to be allowed also.

terms.term: Quando plus fit quam fieri debet, videtur etiam illud fieri quod faciendum est
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When more is done than ought to be done, that shall be considered as performed, which should have been performed; as, if a man having a power to make a lease for ten years, make one for twenty years, it shall be void for the surplus.

terms.term: Quando verba et mens congruunt, non est interpretationi locus
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: When the words and the mind agree, there is no place for interpretation.

terms.term: Qui aliquid staruerit parte inaudita altera, aequum licet dixerit, haud aequum facerit
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who decides anything, a party being unheard, though he should decide right, does wrong.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who distinguishes well, learns well.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who questions well, learns well.

Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who contemns the precept, contemns the party giving it.

terms.term: Qui cum alio contrahit, vel est, vel debet esse non ignarus conditio ejus
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who contracts, knows, or ought to know, the quality of the person with whom he contracts, otherwise he is not excusable.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who destroys the means, destroys the end. 11 Co. 51; Shep.

terms.term: Qui doit inheritoer al pere, doit inheriter al fitz
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who ought to inherit from the father, ought to inherit from the son.

terms.term: Qui evertit causam, evertit causatum futurum
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who overthrows the cause, overthrows its future effects.

terms.term: Qui ex damnato coitu nascuntur, inter liberos non computantur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who is born of an illicit union, is not counted among the children.

terms.term: Qui facit per alium facit per se
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who acts by or through another, acts for himself.

terms.term: Qui habet jurisdictionem absolvendi, habet jurisdictionem ligandi
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who has jurisdiction to loosen, has jurisdiction to bind.

terms.term: Qui haeret in litera, haeret in cortice
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who adheres to the letter, adheres to the bark.

terms.term: Qui ignorat quantum solvere debeat, non potest improbus videre
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does not know what he ought to pay, does not want probity in not paying.

terms.term: Qui in utero est, pro jam nato habetur quoties de ejus commodo quaeritur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who is in the womb, is considered as born, whenever it is for his benefit.

terms.term: Qui jure suo utitur, nemini facit injuriam
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who uses his legal rights, harms no one.

terms.term: Qui jussu judicis aliquod fuerit non videtur dolo malo fecisse, quia parere necesse est
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does anything by command of a judge, will not be supposed to have acted from an improper motive, because it was necessary to obey.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who acts badly, hates the light.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who proves most, recovers most.

terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who betrays his country, is like the insane sailor who bores a hole in the ship which carries him.

terms.term: Qui nascitur sine legitimo matrimonio, matrem sequitur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who is born out of lawful matrimony, follows the condition of the mother.

terms.term: Qui non cadunt in constantem virem, vani timores sunt astinandi
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: Those are vain fears which do not affect a man of a firm mind.

terms.term: Qui non libere veritatem pronunciat, proditor est verilatis
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does not willingly speak the truth, is a betrayer of the truth.

terms.term: Qui non obstat quod obstare potest facere videtur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does not prevent what he can, seems to commit the thing.

terms.term: Qui non prohibit quod prohibere potest assentire videtur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does not forbid what he can forbid, seems to assent.

terms.term: Qui non propulsat injuriam quando potest, infert
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does not repel a wrong when he can, induces it.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who says all, excludes nothing.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who spares the guilty, punishes the innocent.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who offends drunk, must be punished when sober.

terms.term: Qui per alium facit per seipsum facere videtur
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who does anything through another, is considered as doing it himself.

terms.term: Qui per fraudem agit, frustra agit
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who acts fraudulently acts in vain.

terms.term: Qui potest et debet vetare, jubet
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who can and ought to forbid, and does not, commands.

terms.term: Qui primum peccat ille facit rixam
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who first offends, causes the strife.

terms.term: Qui prior est tempore, potior est jure
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who is first or before in time, is stronger in right.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who provides for himself, provides for his heirs.

terms.term: Qui rationem in omnibus quarunt, rationem subvertunt
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who seeks a reason for everything, subverts reason.

terms.term: Qui semel actionem renunciaverit, amplius repetere non potest
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who renounces his action once, cannot any more repeat it.

terms.term: Qui semel malus, semper prasumitur esse malus in eodem genere
terms.definition: Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who is once bad, is presumed to be always so in the same degree.
Bouvier's Law Dictionary (1856), maxim: He who is silent appears to consent.
